text: In the primitive insect societies, conflict and competition lead to the emergence of a single female, the queen, which physically dominates the rest of the adult members of the colony. In the more advanced insect societies, particularly those in which strong differences between the queen and worker castes exist, the queen also exercises control over the workers, but usually in a more subtle manner, without obvious aggression. This evolutionary change, from what might be regarded as rough dominance to the more refined methods of queen control, is one of the clear-cut adaptations that extend across the social insects as a whole, and one worth tracing in some detail.

text: Aggression and dominance were first recorded by the Swiss scientist Pierre Huber (1802) In his pioneering study of bumblebees. He saw that when a queen lays her eggs, some of the workers try to steal and eat them, but the queen usually repels these Intruders with great anger. Similar findings have been reported by a long line of subsequent investigators. The Austrian Eduard Hoffer (1882-1883) discovered that: 'punishment is almost always administered with the legs and mandibles, and the guilty individual never even attempts to defend herself, all her efforts being directed toward making the quickest possible escape. The punishment is sometimes so rough that the poor creature is seriously wounded or even killed.' Once egg stealing has been repelled for a few hours, the attempts by the workers become less and less frequent, and finally cease altogether; and these same little Insects which previously tried 'their very best to get rid of the newly-laid eggs, now become attentive guardians and nurses of their embryo brothers and sisters; they keep them warm and tenderly provide them with nourishment continuously thereafter.'

text: Egg stealing puzzled the early observers; it seemed to them such strange behaviour, as if the bumblebees were heading for race suicide. Huber offered a surprisingly modern hypothesis. He stated: ‘The bumblebees are the largest insects that feed on honey; and if their number trebled or quadrupled, other insects would not find any nourishment, and perhaps their species would be wiped out.' Perez (1899) viewed egg eating as simply evidence of selfish behaviour on the part of the workers, and therefore an Imperfection in the social order. But there is a more straightforward explanation of the phenomenon: Lindhard (1912) observed an Instance In which a queen of the species Bombus lapidaries extracted the egg of a rival worker and fed it to a queen larva. Also noting that very few, if any, worker-laid eggs ever survive, he hypothesized that the objects are not meant to develop but instead provide food for prospective queens. If there is any truth in this conclusion, It Is consistent with the general occurrence of unfertilized eggs laid by workers o related Insect species.

text: At their lowest intensity these encounters are simply a matter of posture; the dominant individual rises on its legs to a level higher than the subordinate, while the subordinate crouches and lowers its antennae. At higher intensities leg biting occurs, and at highest intensity the wasps attempt to sting each other. The severest conflicts occur between wasps of nearly equal rank, and during the early days of the association when the nest is first being constructed. As time passes, the wasps fit more easily into their roles, and aggressive exchanges become more subdued, less frequent, and eventually purely postural in nature. When the first adult workers emerge from the pupa*, during later stages of colony development, their relations to the founders of the colony are invariably subordinate and non-violent. The workers also form a hierarchy among themselves; those that emerge early tend to dominate their younger nestmates. If the head female is removed, the next highest auxiliaries intensify their hostility to each other until one of their number becomes definitely dominant; then the exchanges subside to the previous low level.

text: Eberhard (1969) found that the tropical wasp species Polistes canadensis differs from species found in temperate regions of the world, in that its contests are more violent and result in the losers leaving the nest. The queens are also less dependent on the indirect technique of egg eating to maintain reproductive control. Thus Polistes canadensis approaches a condition of true dictatorship, whereas all the temperate species that have been studied up till now possess a colony organization that can be characterized as an uneasy oligarchy**.
